title: The Butterfly Effect in Space
subtitle: Run the same system twice and find out how long the answer lasts
body:
Step 1 of 28 read

A word that has been worn smooth

On screen are three stars of six solar masses each, sitting at the corners of an equilateral triangle and rotating about their common center like a rigid object. It is not an accident that they fit so neatly: this is an exact solution of the three-body problem, found by Lagrange in 1772, and if the numbers are set up precisely the triangle turns forever without changing shape.

It will not turn forever here. Watch it long enough and it comes apart. That is the subject of this investigation, and the word usually attached to it — chaos — has been worn so smooth by use that it is worth saying at the start what it does not mean.

Chaos does not mean random. It does not mean disordered. It does not mean the computer gave up. It means one specific thing, which you are going to measure: two starts that are almost the same lead to futures that are completely different, and the difference grows exponentially.

Everything in this investigation is aimed at telling that apart from three things it is regularly confused with.

💡 The simulation is paused. Nothing will move until you let it.

title: The Butterfly Effect in Space
subtitle: Run the same system twice and find out how long the answer lasts
body:
Step 28 of 28 read

What you established

In order, and each one measured rather than asserted:

The simulation is deterministic. Two runs from identical starts were identical to every decimal place.

Not all divergence is chaos. A two-body system given the same 1,500 km nudge came apart steadily, in proportion to time. The instrument refused to give it an e-folding time, and was right to.

The three-body system diverged exponentially. The same nudge grew by a factor of e every seven simulated seconds or so — a factor of ten million over the run.

That is physics, not arithmetic. The rate survived halving the timestep and changing the integrator.

And it is not about the number three. Stable three-body configurations exist, and one of them is why Jupiter's Trojan asteroids are still there.
